chunks: Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, both together from Safwan, from Murazim, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

regarding the man who gives something from his wealth during his illness. So he said: 'If he has set it aside (designated it), then it is permissible (valid), and if he bequeathed it, then it is from the one-third (of the estate).'

key_terms.أَبَانَ: to set aside, designate, or separate — in legal context means the person physically segregated the item making it a completed gift (hiba) during their lifetime
key_terms.أَوْصَى: to make a bequest/testament (wasiyya) — a legal directive that takes effect after death
key_terms.الثُّلُثِ: the one-third — Islamic law restricts bequests (wasiyya) to no more than one-third of the estate without heirs' consent

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling in Shia Islam on gifts given by a sick person during their illness — are they counted as gifts or bequests?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses the jurisprudential question of how gifts given by a sick person during their terminal illness (marad al-mawt) are treated in Islamic law. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between two scenarios: if the ill person physically sets aside and designates the gift during their lifetime, the gift is valid and fully enforceable from the whole estate; but if the person merely makes a bequest (wasiyya) for it to be given after death, then it counts against the one-third of the estate that a person is allowed to dispose of by bequest. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential concern for protecting the rights of heirs while honoring the wishes of the deceased.
